name: Web & Browser Security
description: Attacks and defenses for the web platform: browsers, JavaScript, the DOM, web apps, and server-side web code.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from USENIX Security 2018, reflect a web-security field grappling with the consequences of a maturing, JavaScript-heavy platform on both client and server. Several attacked the new server-side reality of Node.js: "Freezing the Web: A Study of ReDoS Vulnerabilities in JavaScript-based Web Servers" (USENIX 2018) and "A Sense of Time for JavaScript and Node.js" (USENIX 2018) showed that a single-threaded event loop made algorithmic-complexity and event-handler-poisoning denial of service unusually easy, a theme echoed by "Rampart: Protecting Web Applications from CPU-Exhaustion Denial-of-Service Attacks" (USENIX 2018). In parallel, classic web-app and protocol weaknesses were being attacked at scale and with automation: "NAVEX" (USENIX 2018) generated exploits for dynamic web apps, while "Efail" (USENIX 2018) and the SSO and third-party-cookie studies ("O Single Sign-Off", "Who Left Open the Cookie Jar?", USENIX 2018) exposed how composed real-world systems — email encryption, federated login, cookie policies — break at their seams. A privacy thread also opened here with "Fp-Scanner" (USENIX 2018) on browser fingerprinting.

By 2019-2020 the field shifted toward systematic defenses and toward treating the browser itself as the security boundary. "Site Isolation: Process Separation for Web Sites within the Browser" (USENIX 2019) was a landmark, putting each site in its own process to contain renderer compromise and side channels — arguably the most consequential architectural defense of the period. Reduction-of-attack-surface thinking appeared in "Less is More: Quantifying the Security Benefits of Debloating Web Applications" (USENIX 2019). The platform also kept expanding, and so did its risks: "Everything Old is New Again: Binary Security of WebAssembly" (USENIX 2020) showed that Wasm reintroduced memory-corruption hazards the web thought it had left behind, while "Montage" (USENIX 2020) advanced neural-network-guided fuzzing of JavaScript engines, signaling the rise of automated bug-finding for browser internals.

The 2021 papers crystallized the realization that the browser is a hardware side-channel surface. "SMASH: Synchronized Many-sided Rowhammer Attacks from JavaScript" (USENIX 2021) and "Prime+Probe 1, JavaScript 0" (USENIX 2021) ran microarchitectural attacks straight from a web page, and "Swivel: Hardening WebAssembly against Spectre" (USENIX 2021) responded by hardening Wasm against Spectre. Alongside this, web-app analysis grew more sophisticated with graph-based program analysis — "JAW" (USENIX 2021) for client-side CSRF and, the next year, "Mining Node.js Vulnerabilities via Object Dependence Graph and Query" (USENIX 2022) and "FUGIO" (USENIX 2022) for PHP object injection. Fingerprinting research matured into a cat-and-mouse around extensions ("Fingerprinting in Style", USENIX 2021).

Most recently the area has split along several mature fronts: privacy-and-policy compliance at web scale ("Automating Cookie Consent and GDPR Violation Detection" and "Leaky Forms", USENIX 2022), deep-learning-based ecosystem defense ("Inferring Phishing Intention via Webpage Appearance and Dynamics", USENIX 2022), the security of blended mobile/web runtimes ("Identity Confusion in WebView-based Mobile App-in-app Ecosystems", USENIX 2022), and increasingly powerful automated bug discovery — "FuzzJIT" (USENIX 2023) targeting JIT compilers and "Atropos" (USENIX 2024) fuzzing server-side PHP web apps. The throughline is clear: what began as point studies of specific bugs has evolved into architectural isolation, hardware-aware threat models, graph-based static analysis, and automated, learning-guided discovery across the full web stack.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this set, all from NDSS 2018, staked out the web platform's classic wound: untrusted code reaching sensitive sinks. "SYNODE: Understanding and Automatically Preventing Injection Attacks on NODE.JS" (NDSS 2018) pushed injection defense down to the server-side JavaScript runtime, while "Riding out DOMsday: Towards Detecting and Preventing DOM Cross-Site Scripting" (NDSS 2018) tackled the browser-side dual, DOM XSS, which had long resisted the taint tracking that server XSS enjoyed. Alongside these, "JavaScript Zero: Real JavaScript and Zero Side-Channel Attacks" (NDSS 2018) treated the language itself as the threat surface, retrofitting the browser to blunt timing and side-channel leaks. The common thread was that the web's attack surface is really the JavaScript engine and DOM, not just the application code layered on top.

That framing drove the field's next breakthrough: fuzzing the engines directly. "CodeAlchemist: Semantics-Aware Code Generation to Find Vulnerabilities in JavaScript Engines" (NDSS 2019) showed that generating semantically valid programs, rather than mutating blindly, could reliably surface engine bugs, and its heavy citation count reflects how it seeded a whole subfield. That line matured through "Favocado: Fuzzing the Binding Code of JavaScript Engines Using Semantically Correct Test Cases" (NDSS 2021), which targeted the neglected binding layer between JS and native code, and culminated in "FUZZILLI: Fuzzing for JavaScript JIT Compiler Vulnerabilities" (NDSS 2023), which reached the JIT compiler itself. A complementary defensive strand ran in parallel, with "NoJITsu: Locking Down JavaScript Engines" (NDSS 2020) hardening engines against the data-only attacks these fuzzers were exposing.

As the engine story deepened, a second axis measured the web as it was actually deployed and tracked users at scale. "Complex Security Policy? A Longitudinal Analysis of Deployed Content Security Policies" (NDSS 2020) documented how poorly the flagship anti-XSS mechanism was adopted in practice, while a run of fingerprinting and tracking papers — "Carnus: Exploring the Privacy Threats of Browser Extension Fingerprinting" (NDSS 2020), "Tales of Favicons and Caches: Persistent Tracking in Modern Browsers" (NDSS 2021), and "DRAWN APART: A Device Identification Technique based on Remote GPU Fingerprinting" (NDSS 2022) — showed trackers repeatedly outflanking browser defenses. Injection also evolved beyond XSS into language-level flaws: "SerialDetector: Principled and Practical Exploration of Object Injection Vulnerabilities for the Web" (NDSS 2021) and "Probe the Proto: Measuring Client-Side Prototype Pollution Vulnerabilities of One Million Real-world Websites" (NDSS 2022) turned prototype pollution and object injection into first-class, internet-scale vulnerability classes, extending SYNODE's server-side concerns into the modern JS ecosystem.

The most recent work, dominated by NDSS 2026, shows the field fragmenting outward from the browser into the sprawl of the modern web stack while carrying its older obsessions forward. Prototype pollution reappears in "Bullseye: Detecting Prototype Pollution in NPM Packages with Proof of Concept Exploits" (NDSS 2026), now demanding working exploits rather than mere reports, and taint analysis climbs into modern frameworks with "TranSPArent: Taint-style Vulnerability Detection in Generic Single Page Applications through Automated Framework Abstraction" (NDSS 2026). Browser architecture itself is under scrutiny in "Are your Sites Truly Isolated? Automatically Detecting Logic Bugs in Site Isolation Implementations" (NDSS 2026), while the platform's boundaries stretch to mobile embeddings in "Cross-Boundary Mobile Tracking: Exploring Java-to-JavaScript Information Diffusion in WebViews" (NDSS 2026) and to backend infrastructure in "The Dark Side of Flexibility: Detecting Risky Permission Chaining Attacks in Serverless Applications" (NDSS 2026). Finally, the arrival of machine learning cuts both ways: "PhishLang: A Real-Time, Fully Client-Side Phishing Detection Framework Using MobileBERT" (NDSS 2026) and "Achieving Interpretable DL-based Web Attack Detection through Malicious Payload Localization" (NDSS 2026) put models on defense, while "ExpShield: Safeguarding Web Text from Unauthorized Crawling and LLM Exploitation" (NDSS 2026) reframes the web page itself as data to be protected from LLMs — a threat model that did not exist when this story began.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection, all from IEEE S&P, is dominated by the tension between users and the tracking-and-advertising economy. FP-STALKER: Tracking Browser Fingerprint Evolutions (S&P 2018) crystallized browser fingerprinting as a cookieless way to follow users without consent, modeling how a device's fingerprint drifts over time so it can still be re-linked. Alongside it, papers like Privacy Risks with Facebook's PII-Based Targeting (S&P 2018) and Surveylance: Automatically Detecting Online Survey Scams (S&P 2018) treated the ad and data-broker ecosystem itself as the attack surface. A parallel strand looked at the platform's own machinery — EmPoWeb: Empowering Web Applications with Browser Extensions (S&P 2019) showed extensions could hand web pages dangerous privileges, while Fidelius: Protecting User Secrets from Compromised Browsers (S&P 2019) and Formally Verified Cryptographic Web Applications in WebAssembly (S&P 2019) pushed toward hardened and formally verified defenses.

Around 2020-2021 the field matured along two lines: regulation-driven measurement and machine learning. Do Cookie Banners Respect my Choice? (S&P 2020), the most-cited paper here, made post-GDPR consent a measurable compliance question, and AdGraph: A Graph-Based Approach to Ad and Tracker Blocking (S&P 2020) reframed blocking as reasoning over a page's execution graph. That graph idea matured into Fingerprinting the Fingerprinters (S&P 2021) and WTAGRAPH: Web Tracking and Advertising Detection using Graph Neural Networks (S&P 2022), which learned to spot tracking behavior rather than hand-writing filter lists — even as Detecting Filter List Evasion (S&P 2021) documented the ensuing cat-and-mouse. Meanwhile the offensive systems side sharpened: Fuzzing JavaScript Engines with Aspect-preserving Mutation (S&P 2020) and Black Widow: Blackbox Data-driven Web Scanning (S&P 2021) automated bug-finding, and Spook.js: Attacking Chrome Strict Site Isolation via Speculative Execution (S&P 2022) showed even Chrome's flagship Site Isolation defense could be broken with Spectre-style speculation.

By 2022-2023 attention turned to concrete web-app and language-level vulnerability classes. Wobfuscator (S&P 2022) weaponized WebAssembly to hide JavaScript malware, the SameSite study (S&P 2022) audited a widely deployed cookie defense, and Toss a Fault to Your Witcher (S&P 2023) brought coverage-guided greybox fuzzing to SQL and command injection in server-side code — a clear step past the blackbox scanners of a few years earlier.

The most recent work marks a decisive pivot toward AI on the web. On the (In)Security of LLM App Stores (S&P 2025) opened the LLM-application security agenda, and the 2026 cohort makes the frontier explicit: When AI Meets the Web: Prompt Injection Risks in Third-Party AI Chatbot Plugins and Investigating the Impact of Dark Patterns on LLM-Based Web Agents probe how agents get manipulated, while WebCloak (S&P 2026) treats LLM agents as a new class of intelligent scrapers to defend against. Most strikingly, Site Isolation is Dead: How Site Isolation is Broken in Agentic Browsers and Extensions (S&P 2026) and State of Browser Process-Isolation: The Same-Site Weakness (S&P 2026) argue that the browser's process-isolation cornerstone — the very defense Spook.js probed years earlier — collapses in the agentic era, even as classic systems work continues with GPU-contention covert channels and the first large-scale study of Python class-pollution vulnerabilities. The area has thus come full circle: from protecting human users against trackers to defending both users and the web platform against, and with, autonomous AI agents.

ccs.narrative:
Web security at CCS has tracked the browser as an expanding attack surface, from script-based tracking to regulatory compliance. The 2018 cohort exposed the browser as an unwilling participant in emerging abuses: MineSweeper: An In-depth Look into Drive-by Cryptocurrency Mining and Its Defense (CCS 2018) and How You Get Shot in the Back: A Systematical Study about Cryptojacking in the Real World (CCS 2018) together documented cryptojacking as a novel browser-native monetization abuse. Mystique: Uncovering Information Leakage from Browser Extensions (CCS 2018) showed that the extension permission model leaks user data broadly, and The Web's Sixth Sense: A Study of Scripts Accessing Smartphone Sensors (CCS 2018) exposed mobile sensor data as a tracking vector.

GDPR compliance became a research topic immediately after the regulation took effect: (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field (CCS 2019) was the defining empirical work, measuring dark patterns across thousands of sites. DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS (CCS 2020) repurposed the TLS handshake to let users prove data provenance to third parties.

Authentication and authorization auditing matured into automated tools. The Cookie Hunter: Automated Black-box Auditing for Web Authentication and Authorization Flaws (CCS 2020) automatically discovered account-access bugs in live web applications. Phishing detection extended into blockchain contexts with TxPhishScope: Towards Detecting and Understanding Transaction-based Phishing on Ethereum (CCS 2023).

milestones.note: Characterized browser-based cryptomining as a distinct threat and built a robust behavioral detector.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, from 2018, splits along two axes that would define web security for years: measuring how the web abuses users, and hardening the code that runs in and behind the browser. On the abuse side, a wave of cryptojacking studies — "MineSweeper: An In-depth Look into Drive-by Cryptocurrency Mining and Its Defense" (CCS 2018) and "How You Get Shot in the Back: A Systematical Study about Cryptojacking in the Real World" (CCS 2018) — quantified a then-new monetization scheme, while a parallel tracking literature (FP-STALKER: Tracking Browser Fingerprint Evolutions, S&P 2018; "The Web's Sixth Sense: A Study of Scripts Accessing Smartphone Sensors" and "Clock Around the Clock: Time-Based Device Fingerprinting," both CCS 2018) showed how scripts fingerprint and follow users without consent. On the code side, injection and DoS moved server-side into Node.js — "SYNODE: Understanding and Automatically Preventing Injection Attacks on NODE.JS" (NDSS 2018) and "Freezing the Web: A Study of ReDoS Vulnerabilities in JavaScript-based Web Servers" (USENIX 2018) — while classic web-app flaws were attacked with automation in "NAVEX: Precise and Scalable Exploit Generation for Dynamic Web Applications" (USENIX 2018) and "Riding out DOMsday: Towards Detecting and Preventing DOM Cross-Site Scripting" (NDSS 2018).

Around 2019–2020 the field matured in two visible ways. First, regulation reshaped the privacy conversation: GDPR turned consent notices themselves into an object of study, from "(Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field" (CCS 2019) to "Do Cookie Banners Respect my Choice?" (S&P 2020), which measured how often banners simply ignore user choices. Second, the browser itself became the battleground for both offense and defense. JavaScript engines drew a sustained fuzzing effort — "CodeAlchemist: Semantics-Aware Code Generation to Find Vulnerabilities in JavaScript Engines" (NDSS 2019), "Fuzzing JavaScript Engines with Aspect-preserving Mutation" (S&P 2020), and "Montage: A Neural Network Language Model-Guided JavaScript Engine Fuzzer" (USENIX 2020) — while "Site Isolation: Process Separation for Web Sites within the Browser" (USENIX 2019) documented Chrome's architectural answer to cross-origin memory disclosure. New execution substrates got early scrutiny too, as in "Everything Old is New Again: Binary Security of WebAssembly" (USENIX 2020), and graph- and ML-based defenses appeared against tracking (AdGraph, S&P 2020; "Fingerprinting the Fingerprinters," S&P 2021).

The early 2020s pushed the browser as a hardware side-channel and attack surface in its own right. "SMASH: Synchronized Many-sided Rowhammer Attacks from JavaScript" (USENIX 2021) triggered Rowhammer bit flips straight from a web page, and "Prime+Probe 1, JavaScript 0: Overcoming Browser-based Side-Channel Defenses" (USENIX 2021) defeated the very timer and isolation defenses browsers had deployed against cache attacks. Meanwhile the applied-web-security frontier kept moving up the stack toward auditing real deployments — "The Cookie Hunter: Automated Black-box Auditing for Web Authentication and Authorization Flaws" (CCS 2020) — and toward vision- and learning-based phishing detection ("Inferring Phishing Intention via Webpage Appearance and Dynamics," USENIX 2022).

The most recent work, clustered at NDSS 2026, shows a field grappling with modern web complexity and with LLMs on both sides. Framework-level analysis has become necessary: "TranSPArent: Taint-style Vulnerability Detection in Generic Single Page Applications" and "Bullseye: Detecting Prototype Pollution in NPM Packages with Proof of Concept Exploits" chase bugs that live in today's SPA and npm ecosystems, while "Are your Sites Truly Isolated? Automatically Detecting Logic Bugs in Site Isolation Implementations" stress-tests the very isolation defense introduced back in 2019. The mobile/web boundary resurfaces in "Cross-Boundary Mobile Tracking: Exploring Java-to-JavaScript Information Diffusion in WebViews," and serverless brings new flaws in "The Dark Side of Flexibility: Detecting Risky Permission Chaining Attacks in Serverless Applications." Most tellingly, large language models now define the newest threats and tools — "ExpShield: Safeguarding Web Text from Unauthorized Crawling and LLM Exploitation" defends content against LLM scraping, while "PhishLang: A Real-Time, Fully Client-Side Phishing Detection Framework Using MobileBERT" and "Achieving Interpretable DL-based Web Attack Detection through Malicious Payload Localization" put deep learning directly into client-side and interpretable web defense.
